snip.t: These indicate central nervous system (CNS) infections like cryptococcal meningitis, cerebral toxoplasmosis, or tuberculoma.

Neurological signs: Meningism (often subtle in cryptococcal meningitis due to blunted inflammatory response), focal motor/sensory deficits (focal toxoplasma abscesses or tuberculoma), or cranial nerve palsies (basal tuberculous meningitis).
Subacute onset over 1–2 weeks points toward tuberculous or cryptococcal meningitis.
| Cryptococcal meningitis | CD4 < 200, indolent onset, minimal neck signs | Positive India ink or CrAg test |
Crucial for CNS infections (e.g., Cryptococcal meningitis, cerebral toxoplasmosis, neurocysticercosis, cerebral malaria).
Neck stiffness: Meningeal irritation (e.g., Cryptococcal meningitis, cerebral toxoplasmosis).
*TB meningitis* vs. *cryptococcal meningitis* – CSF opening pressure very high in cryptococcal; India‑ink positive.
Infectious: Cerebral malaria, tuberculous meningitis, cryptococcal meningitis, HIV‑related opportunistic infections — Recent travel, immunosuppression, poor malaria prophylaxis

ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Cryptococcal meningitis is a life‑threatening fungal infection of the meninges, most common in immunocompromised patients, especially HIV. Early recognition, CSF testing and prompt antifungal therapy are essential to reduce mortality.

sections.p: Cryptococcus neoformans (and C. gattii) are encapsulated yeasts that can cross the blood‑brain barrier and cause meningitis. The disease presents with subacute headache, fever, and meningeal signs, often mimicking tuberculous meningitis.
b: Most common meningitis in AIDS patients

sections.p: Encapsulated yeast, 5–7 µm, reproduces by budding. The polysaccharide capsule (glucuronoxylomannan) is key to immune evasion and is detected by India ink stain.
b: Capsule → false‑negative cultures if not processed promptly

sections.p: Inhalation of desiccated yeast or spores from soil contaminated with bird droppings initiates pulmonary infection; hematogenous spread reaches the CNS.
b: Environmental exposure common in tropical and temperate regions
HIV, steroids, organ transplant increase risk

sections.p: Cryptococcal meningitis presents with headache, fever, neck stiffness, photophobia, and altered mental status. It can progress to hydrocephalus, cerebral edema, and death if untreated.
b: Can cause cryptococcal antigenemia without meningitis

sections.p: CSF analysis is central; rapid antigen detection and culture confirm the diagnosis.
b: India ink shows capsule in CSF
Cryptococcal antigen (CrAg) lateral flow assay is highly sensitive

t.b: Is intracranial hypertension present? High pressure (>250 mm H₂O) predicts need for therapeutic lumbar puncture
Does it show encapsulated yeast? Positive confirms infection
Is antigen present? Positive even with low organism load
Grows yeast in 3–7 days; definitive but may be unavailable—use CrAg instead

sections.p: Induction with amphotericin B plus flucytosine for at least two weeks, followed by fluconazole consolidation and maintenance. Manage intracranial pressure aggressively.
b: Fluconazole → oral, good CNS levels for long‑term suppression
Therapeutic lumbar puncture if opening pressure >250 mm H₂O

sections.p: Key points to remember for exams and clinical practice.
b: Cryptococcal meningitis = most common AIDS meningitis
Positive CrAg in serum or CSF is diagnostic
High CSF opening pressure requires repeated LPs

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly worsening headache, fever, neck stiffness, or altered consciousness in an immunocompromised patient

faq.q: Why is the cryptococcal antigen test preferred over culture?
faq.a: It gives results within minutes, is highly sensitive even with low fungal burden, and works when cultures are unavailable.

faq.q: Can cryptococcal meningitis occur in HIV‑negative patients?
faq.a: Yes, especially with C. gattii exposure, organ transplantation, or chronic steroid use.

faq.q: What is the main cause of death in cryptococcal meningitis?
faq.a: Raised intracranial pressure leading to brain herniation.
